Header-based routing (SEP-2243) requires requests to include `Mcp-Method` and `Mcp-Name` headers so gateways and load balancers can route without parsing JSON bodies. Clinton proposes four questions for evaluating an agent deployment: (1) does it ingest untrusted content (external email, web content or third-party documents an attacker could write or modify)? (2) action scope and identity — what capabilities does it have and under whose authorization does it act? (3) blast radius — would misalignment affect a single file, departmental data or enterprise-wide systems? (4) observability — can you distinguish agent actions from user actions in your SIEM? The core argument is that zero risk isn't the job — CISOs should make risk legible and bounded so it becomes a deliberate acceptance rather than reactive governance.

2026-07-06|research|anthropic.com: Anthropic publishes "A global workspace in language models" — J-Space discovered inside Claude — On 2026-07-06 Anthropic posted a new research paper in its official research section introducing a novel interpretability tool called the Jacobian lens (J-lens), which uncovered a small but important "privileged workspace" inside Claude that the company dubs J-space. The J-lens works by computing the average mathematical effect of a given internal activation pattern on the model's future output of specific tokens. J-space has three key properties: (1) it is tiny — holding only "a few dozen" concepts at a time and accounting for less than a tenth of the model's overall activity, yet carrying most of the work that matters for safety; (2) it is observable and interveneable — Claude can report the contents of J-space when asked and can modulate them on request, and researchers can causally alter Claude's outputs and task performance by intervening directly in J-space; (3) it emerges from training — the activation patterns were not hand-designed but arose spontaneously during training. The authors draw a parallel to Bernard Baars' neuroscience global-workspace theory — the brain as a theater with many parallel processors working backstage while only a small "spotlight" of information gets broadcast to the whole theater and becomes conscious content. Anthropic emphasizes that the research "does not claim Claude is conscious" and "does not claim Claude has subjective experience," warns against reading it as "AI is alive" clickbait, and positions J-space as a key entry point for future detection of misalignment and scheming.

Delba de Oliveira and Michael Segner of the Claude Code team published the guide on the claude.com blog, defining loops as "agents repeating cycles of work until a stop condition is met" and categorizing them by trigger and stop condition into four types: turn-based loops (triggered by user prompts, stopping when Claude judges the work complete or needs more context — best for shorter, non-recurring tasks), goal-based loops (/goal, manually triggered, stopping when verifiable exit criteria are met or max turns are reached — suited to tasks with clear success conditions), time-based loops (/loop and /schedule, triggered on specified intervals — suited to recurring work and monitoring external systems), and proactive loops (event- or schedule-triggered with no real-time human involvement, composing subagents and dynamic workflows for well-defined always-on work). Selection guidance: start with the simplest solution and use loops selectively; replace subjective judgments with quantifiable, deterministic success criteria to cut token usage and iterations. For quality, encode verification standards as skills and use a secondary agent for code review; for token management, pick primitives and models per task, pilot dynamic workflows on smaller data slices, use scripts for deterministic operations, match routine intervals to actual change frequency, and monitor usage via the /usage, /goal, and /workflows commands. Examples include "/goal get the homepage Lighthouse score to 90 or above, stop after 5 tries.".

2026-06-03|claude-code|claude.com: Anthropic published "Lessons from building Claude Code: How we use skills" on the claude.com blog — the Claude Code team shares how they build and use skills internally. Key points: skills are "folders of instructions, scripts, and resources" that agents can discover and invoke to do things more accurately and efficiently, not merely markdown files; the team identifies nine categories of skills used inside Anthropic (from library references to infrastructure operations). Six core practices: (1) Don't state the obvious — focus on information that pushes Claude beyond its default behavior; (2) Build a Gotchas section — the highest-signal content in any skill is the Gotchas capturing Claude's common failure points; (3) Use file-system structure for progressive disclosure — organized folders with references/scripts/examples instead of one monolithic document; (4) Give Claude flexibility — provide necessary information but let the model adapt rather than over-specifying procedures; (5) Leverage persistent memory — store data in text logs or JSON via the `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}` environment variable so Claude can reference its own history; (6) Include utility scripts — prebuilt code libraries let Claude focus on composition and decisions rather than reconstructing boilerplate. The team also tracks skill usage via PreToolUse hooks to measure effectiveness and identify popular versus underperforming skills.

2026-03-25|claude-code|anthropic.com: Anthropic engineering blog "How we built Claude Code auto mode: a safer way to skip permissions" (by John Hughes) details auto mode's security architecture. Auto mode sits between approving every action manually (users approve ~93% anyway, causing fatigue) and disabling safeguards entirely, instead delegating risky-action decisions to AI classifiers. Two defensive layers: (1) Input-layer prompt-injection defense -- a server-side probe screens tool outputs (file reads, web fetches, shell results) before they enter the agent's context; on suspicious content it injects a warning telling the agent to verify user intent rather than execute injected instructions. (2) Output-layer action gating -- a transcript classifier evaluates each action before execution in two stages (a fast single-token filter that errs toward blocking, then detailed reasoning only when flagged), balancing safety and cost. Key design: the classifier sees only user messages and raw tool commands -- not the agent's reasoning or tool outputs -- preventing persuasive rationalizations and eliminating the main injection vector. Three-tier permission model: built-in safe-tool allowlist (reads, searches, navigation) / in-project file ops (reviewable via version control) / high-risk actions (shell commands, external calls, out-of-project file ops) requiring classifier review. Metrics: false-positive rate on real traffic 8.5%->0.4% after stage 2; false-negative rate on genuinely dangerous actions 6.6%->17%; synthetic-exfiltration recall 1.8%->5.7%. The 17% FNR reflects the core limitation -- judging whether user consent covers a dangerous command's blast radius. Blocked actions return as a tool result instructing the agent to find safer alternatives; sessions escalate to humans only after 3 consecutive denials or 20 total blocks, avoiding cascading failures from false positives. Anthropic states this is not a drop-in replacement for careful human review on high-stakes infrastructure, targeting users who would otherwise fully bypass permissions.
